prompt: I would like to outperform the S&P 500 in the next year. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy?
reply:
Here are 10 stocks to research, with the reasoning and main risk for each. Two caveats first:

- **Beating the S&P 500 is hard.** In most years, most professional large-cap fund managers fail to beat it, and over 15+ years roughly 9 in 10 fall short. A 10-stock portfolio can beat the index, but it can also trail it badly.
- **My information runs through about May 2026.** Prices, valuations and news have changed since then, so check current numbers before buying. This is not personalized financial advice.

## 10 stocks to research

| # | Ticker | Company | Why it could outperform | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NVDA** | NVIDIA | Dominant in AI accelerators, with a strong software ecosystem (CUDA) and high margins | AI spending slowing; custom chips taking share; export limits to China |
| 2 | **TSM** | Taiwan Semiconductor | Makes nearly all leading-edge AI chips for NVIDIA, Apple, AMD and Broadcom; not in the S&P 500, so it sets you apart from the index | Taiwan geopolitical risk; a downturn in the chip cycle |
| 3 | **AVGO** | Broadcom | Custom AI chips for hyperscalers plus AI networking; steady software cash flow from VMware | High valuation; revenue concentrated in a few large customers |
| 4 | **GOOGL** | Alphabet | Google Cloud growth, its own TPU chips, Gemini, YouTube, and a historically lower valuation than its mega-cap peers | AI chatbots eating into search; antitrust remedies |
| 5 | **META** | Meta Platforms | AI is making its ad targeting and engagement better; very profitable | Very high AI spending; regulation; costs of its Reality Labs division |
| 6 | **AMZN** | Amazon | AWS benefiting from AI demand; rising retail margins; a fast-growing ads business | Heavy spending weighing on free cash flow; pressure on consumer spending |
| 7 | **LLY** | Eli Lilly | Leader in GLP-1 obesity and diabetes drugs, with an oral pill (orforglipron) that could widen the market | Drug price pressure; competition; high valuation |
| 8 | **GEV** | GE Vernova | Surging electricity demand from data centers; gas turbines and grid equipment sold out years ahead | The stock has already risen a lot; execution risk; its wind business |
| 9 | **JPM** | JPMorgan Chase | Best-in-class bank that earns strongly across rate environments; adds balance outside tech | A credit downturn or recession |
| 10 | **BRK.B** | Berkshire Hathaway | Stabilizes the portfolio: a huge cash pile ready for buying opportunities, and a mix of insurance, railroad and energy businesses | Tends to lag in strong bull markets; the leadership change from Buffett to Greg Abel |

## Why this might or might not beat the index

**How it could win:**
- It concentrates on what I see as the strongest long-term trends: AI infrastructure, electricity demand and obesity drugs.
- It holds far fewer weak businesses than a 500-stock index.

**How it could lose:**
- **It overlaps heavily with the S&P 500.** The biggest tech stocks already make up roughly a third of the index. Where you overlap, you mostly match the index; the non-index names like TSM do the differentiating.
- **It is a concentrated bet on AI.** About 6 of the 10 stocks depend on AI spending continuing. If that spending cycle pauses, these stocks could fall together and lag the index.

## Practical tips

1. **Size your positions deliberately.** Weight each stock equally (10% each) and rebalance once or twice a year. That stops one winner from quietly taking over the portfolio.
2. **Consider a core-and-satellite approach.** For example, put 70–80% in an S&P 500 index fund and 20–30% in these picks. You still get a chance to outperform without betting everything on it.
3. **Mind taxes.** In the US, gains on stocks held under a year are taxed at your higher ordinary income rate, which can cancel out a small lead over the index.
4. **Set your rules in advance.** Decide now what would make you sell each stock (for example, "the reason I bought it no longer holds"), so you don't react emotionally to price swings.

If you tell me your risk tolerance, how long you plan to invest and whether you prefer growth or value, I can tailor the list. I could also write a script that tracks these picks against the S&P 500 over time.
